'''arytenoid''' (ar-i-tē′noid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< NL. ''arytænoides,'' < Gr. ἀρυταινοειδής, < ἀρύταινα, fem. form of ἀρυτήρ, a ladle or cup (< ἀρύειν, draw water), + εἶδος, form.] '''I.''' ''a.'' cent, has been reduced to ''as''. ''As'' is thus historically ''so'' with an absorbed intensive, whose force has disappeared; and it has all the relational uses of ''so'', the differences being only idiomatical. The peculiar form and uses of ''as'' have arisen out of the correlation ''so'' . . . ''so'' (AS. ''swā'' . . . ''swā'', or, without separation, ''swā swā''), in which both terms were orig. demonstrative. The second term passed into the relative use, and the first, remaining demonstrative, was strengthened by the adv. ''all'' (AS. ''eal swā'' . . . ''swā''). The second term, as a relative, became weak in accent, and, after assuming the prefix ''all'' in conformity to the first, was gradually reduced, through ''also'', ''alse'', ''als'', ''ase'', to ''as'', to which, in turn, the first term in many constructions conformed. The resulting correlations ''so'' . . . ''so'', ''so'' . . . ''as'', ''as'' . . . ''so'', ''as'' . . . ''as'', through involution of uses, transposition of clauses, and ellipsis of one or the other term, extending often to the whole clause, present in mod. E. a complication of constructions which cannot be fully exhibited except at great length, and in connection with the earlier uses. They are also involved with the kindred correlations ''such'' . . . ''as'' (''such'' being historically ''so'', with an absorbed relational suffix) and ''same'' . . . ''as'', in which the relative conj. ''as'' varies with ''that'', and leads to the use of ''as'' as a simple relative pronoun.]

'''Arya''' (är′yä̤), ''n.''   [Skt. ''Ārya'': see ''Aryan''.]   Same as ''Aryan''.
{{smaller block|But besides these ''Aryas'' there were also the Dasyus, of whom we learn little but that they were dark in complexion and constantly at war with the ''Aryas''.
{{right|''J. Robson'', Hinduism, p. 13.}}}}

'''Aryan''' (är′yan or ar′ịan), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Also written ''Arian'', after L. ''Ariānus'', belonging to ''Ariana'' or ''Aria'', Gr. Ἀρεία, Ἀρία, or Ἄρια, the eastern part of ancient Persia, < Skt. ''Ārya'', the name by which the Sanskrit-speaking immigrants into India called themselves, in distinction from the aborigines of the country, whom they called ''Dasyu'', ''Śudra'', etc. The ancient Persians gave themselves the same title (OPers. ''Ariya'', Zend ''Airya''); and it appears in the name of their country, ''Airyana'' or ''Īrān'': see ''Iranic''. There are no traces of the word to be found outside of these two races. Its origin is obscure and disputed; there is no probability that it has anything to do with a root *''ar'', plow.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the Aryans or to their speech. See II.
{{smaller block|Our faith, our customs, our language, were all but fragments of the primitive ''Aryan'' stock common to Rome and Germany.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 118.}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A member of the eastern or Asiatic division of the Indo-European family, occupying the territories between Mesopotamia and the Bay of Bengal, in the two subdivisions of Persia, or Iran, and India. {{smaller|[This is the older, more scientific, and still widely current use of the word. More recent, but increasingly popular, is the second use.]}} '''2.''' An Indo-European or Indo-German or Japhetite; a member of that section of the human race which includes the Hindus and Iranians (Persians) as its eastern or Asiatic division, and the Greeks, Italians, Celts, Slavonians, and Germans or Teutons as its western or European division. {{smaller|The languages of all these branches or groups of peoples are akin; that is to say, they are descendants of one original tongue, once spoken in a limited locality by a single community, but where or when it is impossible to say.}}
{{smaller block|Many words still live in India and England that have witnessed the first separation of the northern and southern ''Aryans'', and these are witnesses not to be shaken by any cross-examination. The terms for God, for house, for father, mother, son, daughter, for dog and cow, for heart and tears, for axe and tree, identical in all the Indo-European idioms, are like the watchwords of soldiers. We challenge the seeming stranger; and whether he answer with the lips of a Greek, a German, or an Indian, we recognize him as one of ourselves. There was a time when the ancestors of the Celts, the Germans, the Slavonians, the Greeks and Italians, the Persians and Hindus, were living together beneath the same roof, separate from the ancestors of the Semitic and Turanian races.
{{right|''Max Müller.''}}}}

'''Aryandic''' (är-yan′dik), ''a.'' Originating with Aryandes, Persian satrap of Egypt, condemned to death by Darius for coining silver finer than that of the great king himself.—'''Aryandic coin,''' {{smaller|a coin struck by Aryandes.}}

'''Aryanize''' (är′yan-īz or ar′ian-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''Aryanized'', ppr. ''Aryänizing''.   [< ''Aryan'' + ''-ize''.]   To render Aryan in character or appearance; impart Aryan peculiarities to. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|European artists who have not lived among the African race sometimes try their hands at a pretty negress, but they always ''Aryanize'' the type.
{{right|''G. Allen'', Physiol. Æsthetics, p. 241.}}}}

'''aryballus''' (ar-i-bal′us), ''n.''; pl. ''aryballi'' (-ī).   [< Gr. ἀρύβαλλος, a bag or purse made so as to draw {{img float|file=century v01 p0356 c1f1.png|width=123px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Archaic Aryballus.}}}} close, a vessel so shaped.]   In ''archæol.'', a form of Greek vase. {{smaller|Probably in ancient times this name was applied to a large vase with a small neck, used for carrying water to the bath. In modern archæological nomenclature, it generally denotes a small vase shaped like a ball, with a short neck and a small orifice surrounded}} by a broad flat rim, used like the alabastrum in anointing the body with oil.

'''aryepiglottic''' (ar″i-ep-i-glot′ik), ''a.''   [< ''ary''(''tenoid'') + ''epiglottic.'']   Same as ''aryteno-epiglottic.''
{{smaller block|Folds of mucous membrane, extending from the epiglottis to the arytenoid cartilages, are the ''aryepiglottic'' ligaments.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 93.}}}}

'''aryepiglottidean''' (ar-i-ep″i-glo-tid′ẹ̄-a̤n), ''a.'' Same as ''aryteno-epiglottic.''

'''aryteno-epiglottic''' (ar-i-tē″nō-ep-i-glot′ik), ''a.''   [< ''aryteno''(''id'') + ''epiglottic.'']   In ''anat.'', pertaining to the arytenoid cartilages and the epiglottis.—'''Aryteno-epiglottic fold,''' {{smaller|one of two folds of mucous membrane passing from the tips of the arytenoid cartilages and the cornicula laryngis to the lateral margins of the epiglottis.}}

'''aryteno-epiglottidean''' (ar-i-tē″nō-ep″i-glo-tid′ẹ̄-a̤n), ''a.''   [< ''aryteno-epiglottideus'' + ''-an.'']   Same as ''aryteno-epiglottic.''

'''aryteno-epiglottideus''' (ar-i-tē″nō-ep″i-glo-tid′ẹ̄-us), ''n.''; pl. ''aryteno-epiglottidei'' (-ī).   [NL.]   The name of one of two pairs of small muscles of the larynx extending from the arytenoid cartilages to or toward the epiglottis.—'''Aryteno-epiglottideus inferior,''' {{smaller|muscular fibers arising from the arytenoid cartilages and spreading out upon the laryngeal pouch, which is compressed by the action of the muscle. Also called ''compressor sacculi laryngis.''}}—'''Aryteno-epiglottideus superior,''' {{smaller|a few muscular fibers extending from the apex of the arytenoid cartilages to the aryteno-epiglottidean fold of mucous membrane.}}

'''arytenoglottidean''' (ar-i-tē″nō-glo-tid′ẹ̄-a̤n), ''a.'' Same as ''aryteno-epiglottic.''

'''arytenoid''' (ar-i-tē′noid), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< NL. ''arytænoides,'' < Gr. ἀρυταινοειδής, < ἀρύταινα, fem. form of ἀρυτήρ, a ladle or cup (< ἀρύειν, draw water), + εἶδος, form.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Ladle- or cup-shaped: in ''anat.,'' applied to two small cartilages at the top of the larynx, and also to the muscles connected with these cartilages.—{{smaller|'''Arytenoid cartilages.''' See ''cartilage.''—'''Arytenoid gland.''' See ''gland.''—'''Arytenoid muscle.''' Same as ''arytenoideus.''}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' An arytenoid cartilage.

'''arytenoidal''' (ar″i-tẹ̄-noi′da̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''arytenoid.''

'''arytenoideus''' (ar″i-tẹ̄-noi′dẹ̄-us), ''n.''; pl. ''arytenoidei'' (-ī).   [NL.: see ''arytenoid.'']   The arytenoid muscle, a muscle of the larynx passing transversely behind the arytenoid cartilages from one to the other.—{{smaller|'''Arytenoideus major,''' the arytenoideus.—'''Arytenoideus minor.''' Same as ''arytenoideus obliquus.''—'''Arytenoideus obliquus,''' two small oblique bundles of muscular fibers crossing behind the arytenoid cartilages, regarded as parts of the aryteno-epiglottidean muscles.—'''Arytenoideus transversus,''' the arytenoideus.}}

'''as<sup>1</sup>''' (az), ''adv.'', ''conj.'', and ''pron.''   [< ME. ''as, ase, als, alse, also, alsa, alswa, al so, al swa,'' < AS. ''alswā, ealswā, eal swā'' (= OS. ''alsō'' = OFries. ''as, ase, asa, als, alse, alsa'' = D. ''als'' = OHG. ''alsō,'' MHG. ''alsō, alse,'' G. ''alsō, als''), lit. ‘all so,’ wholly so, quite so, just so, being the demonstrative adv. ''so,'' qualified by the intensive adv. ''all.'' As a demonstrative, the word retains its full form (see ''also''); as a relative or correlative, the word, through weakening of force and accent, has been reduced to ''as''. ''As'' is thus historically ''so'' with an absorbed intensive, whose force has disappeared; and it has all the relational uses of ''so'', the differences being only idiomatical. The peculiar form and uses of ''as'' have arisen out of the correlation ''so'' . . . ''so'' (AS. ''swā'' . . . ''swā'', or, without separation, ''swā swā''), in which both terms were orig. demonstrative. The second term passed into the relative use, and the first, remaining demonstrative, was strengthened by the adv. ''all'' (AS. ''eal swā'' . . . ''swā''). The second term, as a relative, became weak in accent, and, after assuming the prefix ''all'' in conformity to the first, was gradually reduced, through ''also'', ''alse'', ''als'', ''ase'', to ''as'', to which, in turn, the first term in many constructions conformed. The resulting correlations ''so'' . . . ''so'', ''so'' . . . ''as'', ''as'' . . . ''so'', ''as'' . . . ''as'', through involution of uses, transposition of clauses, and ellipsis of one or the other term, extending often to the whole clause, present in mod. E. a complication of constructions which cannot be fully exhibited except at great length, and in connection with the earlier uses. They are also involved with the kindred correlations ''such'' . . . ''as'' (''such'' being historically ''so'', with an absorbed relational suffix) and ''same'' . . . ''as'', in which the relative conj. ''as'' varies with ''that'', and leads to the use of ''as'' as a simple relative pronoun.]

'''I.''' ''adv.'' (''demonstrative'' or ''antecedent''). The antecedent in the correlation ''as'' . . . ''so'', or ''as'' . . . ''as'': In that degree; to that extent; so far. {{smaller|The correlation ''as'' . . . ''so'' is obsolete; ''as'' . . . ''as'' is in extremely common use, being, besides ''like'', the regular formula}} of comparison to express likeness or equality: as, ''as'' black ''as'' jet, ''as'' cold ''as'' ice, ''as'' wise ''as'' Solomon, etc.; the {{smaller block|verb in the relative clause, when the same as in the principal clause, being usually omitted: as, it is ''as'' cold ''as'' ice (sc. is); come ''as'' soon ''as'' you can (sc. come).}}

{{smaller block|He was ''al so'' [var. ''also'', ''als'', ''as''] fresche ''as'' is the moneth of Mai.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 92.}}}}

<poem>Lo! whiche sleightes and subtiltees
In wommen ben! for ay ''as'' bisy ''as'' bees
Ben they, vs sely men for to deceyve.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire’s Tale, Prol., l. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|We [Americans] use these words [faith and hope] as if they were ''as'' obsolete ''as'' Selah and Amen.
{{right|''Emerson'', Man the Reformer.}}}}

{{smaller block|The relative clause is often omitted, especially in colloquial speech, being inferred from the antecedent: as, this will do ''as'' well (sc. ''as'' that); I would ''as'' lief walk (sc. ''as'' ride).}}

<poem>The bad man shall attend ''as'' bad a master.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, v. 3.}}}}

<poem>I will be temperate
In speaking, and ''as'' just in hearing.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iv. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|These scruples to many perhaps seem pretended, to others, upon ''as'' good grounds, may seem real.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xi.}}}}

{{smaller block|The appointment of a regular wit has long ceased to be a part of the economy of a morning paper. Editors find their own jokes, or do ''as'' well without them.
{{right|''Lamb'', Newspapers 35 Years Ago.}}}}

'''II.''' ''conj.'' (''conjunctive'' or ''relative adv.''). '''1.''' The consequent in the correlations ''as'' . . . ''as'', ''so'' . . . ''as'', ''such'' . . . ''as'', ''same'' . . . ''as'', etc., expressing quantity, degree, proportion, manner, etc. {{smaller|The relative uses are as exhibited in I. (where see examples). Through ellipsis of the antecedent, it enters into many peculiar idiomatic phrases.}}

{{smaller block|No, ’tis not ''so'' deep ''as'' a well, nor ''so'' wide ''as'' a church-door; but ’tis enough, ’twill serve.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|His resolutions were ''as'' fained ''as'' his vows were frustrate.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxv.}}}}

{{smaller block|The results of this campaign were ''as'' honorable to Spain ''as'' they were disastrous and humiliating to Louis the Twelfth.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 13.}}}}

The clauses may be transposed for emphasis.

{{smaller block|''As'' thy days, ''so'' shall thy strength be. Deut. xxxiii. 25.}}

{{smaller block|''As'' it is in particular persons, ''so'' it is in nations.
{{right|''Bacon'', Atheism.}}}}

The antecedent ''as'' is often, and ''so'' is usually, omitted: as, black ''as'' jet; cold ''as'' ice; do ''as'' you like.

<poem>The motions of his spirit are dull ''as'' night,
And his affections dark ''as'' Erebus.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., v. 1.}}}}

<poem>I desire no titles,
But ''as'' I shall deserve ’em.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Prophetess, ii. 3.}}}}

<poem>Black it stood ''as'' night,
Fierce ''as'' ten furies, terrible ''as'' hell.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 671.}}}}

{{smaller block|I live ''as'' I did, I think ''as'' I did, I love you ''as'' I did.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}

{{smaller block|It is in criticism, ''as'' in all other Sciences and Speculations.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 291.}}}}

In parenthetical clauses involving a concession, the relative ''as'' (the antecedent being omitted) may be equivalent to ''though'': as, late ''as'' it was, we set forth on our journey.

{{smaller block|Trite ''as'' the counsel was, . . . in this emergency it was to me as if an angel had spoken.
{{right|''Lamb'', Amicus Redivivus.}}}}

{{smaller block|Neither the arguments nor entreaties of his friends, backed ''as'' they were by the avowed wishes of his sovereign, could overcome his scruples.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 5.}}}}

{{smaller block|In parenthetical clauses involving a contrast or negation as to fact with the principal clause, ''as'' approaches an adversative sense, being nearly equivalent to ''but''.}}

<poem>Had I but time, (''as'' this fell sergeant, Death,
Is strict in his arrest,) O, I could tell you,—
But let it be.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|I must confess I lov’d her; ''as'' who would not?
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, v. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|In subordinate clauses involving a supposition, ''as'' is conditional, being equivalent to ''as if'', ''as though'', which are the ordinary forms. This use is now rare or only poetical except in the independent phrase ''as it were''. (See phrases below.)}}

<poem>It lifted up its head, and did address
Itself to motion, like ''as'' it would speak.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2.}}}}

<poem>And all at once their breath drew in,
''As'' they were drinking all.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Coleridge'', Ancient Mariner, l. 165.}}}}

<poem>The young lambs bound
''As'' to the tabor’s sound.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Intimations of Immortality.}}}}

{{smaller block|The clause introduced by ''as'' may be reduced by ellipsis of its verb and other elements to one or two important words, leaving ''as'' as a quasi-connective: (''a'') Between an adverb or adverbial phrase in the principal clause and an adverb or adverbial phrase constituting the subordinate clause.}}

{{smaller block|It suffices me to say . . . that men here, ''as'' elsewhere, are indisposed to innovation.
{{right|''Emerson'', Lit. Ethics.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''b'') Between the principal verb or its subject and the subordinate subject or object, which becomes equivalent to a predicate appositive or factitive object after the principal}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
